prize_parts.citation: for discoveries in GLP-1 physiology and the development of GLP-1-based therapies for type 2 diabetes and obesity

statement.case_for: All six of us placed GLP-1 first, but unanimity is not what carries the case. What does is a discernible change in the field: gut-hormone physiology (proglucagon processing, the insulinotropic and satiety actions of GLP-1(7-36)) became a drug class that has changed how type 2 diabetes and obesity are treated and now shows cardiovascular and renal benefit in large independent outcome trials. The chain from mechanism to patient is unusually clear, and after three decades of basic work and more than a decade of clinical experience the maturity question is settled. I keep Holst and Drucker for the physiology and Knudsen for turning that physiology into degradation-resistant, long-acting agonists, because the prize is for a discovery that reached patients, and a prize limited to the hormone biology would omit the step that made it matter.
statement.case_against: The strongest objection is attribution. Mojsov's contribution to identifying the active GLP-1(7-36) peptide is real, and Habener, who is not among the credited names, is part of the early story, so the three-person cap forces a contested exclusion whichever trio is chosen. Knudsen's work was done in an industrial setting, and whether it counts as discovery rather than development is a legitimate dispute. If the committee decides the prize should recognise physiology only, my configuration is the wrong one and the Drucker, Holst and Mojsov trio proposed by El Manira, Linnarsson and Sandberg would be more defensible. A second reservation is that GLP-1 will win almost by default because of the opening ballots, which tells us little about whether the laureate set is right.

responses.point: El Manira, with Linnarsson and Sandberg, proposes Drucker, Holst and Mojsov for B025 and leaves Knudsen out because her work is industrial and translational and the prize should stay on discovery.
responses.response: I take this seriously, and it is the closest call in this prize. My difficulty is that identifying the active peptide, while important, was a step in characterising the hormone, whereas the decisive change in medicine came from making the peptide pharmacologically usable, which is Knudsen's contribution. Mojsov's priority claim is also disputed in a way I cannot resolve from the supplied record, and I do not want the prize to rest on a contested priority when a clearly documented contribution is available. I would move if the committee agrees the prize should be about physiology alone, but not merely to avoid industry credit.

responses.point: Svenningsson ranks B038 second and B020 third, proposes Drucker, Holst and Knudsen for GLP-1, and for CAR-T proposes only June and Sadelain, treating engineering of the receptor as the core discovery and Rosenberg as a different contribution.
responses.response: On GLP-1 we agree on the trio. On CAR-T I partly disagree: I included Rosenberg because adoptive cell transfer is the conceptual basis for what June and Sadelain engineered. But I accept that two names give a cleaner configuration, given that Eshhar's early chimeric receptor is already missing from the list, and I would not defend the third seat. On B038 I am less convinced than you that it belongs second; the six-name dispute among Bamberg, Boyden, Deisseroth, Hegemann, Miesenboeck and Nagel is a serious fairness problem, and I rank it below the mechanism-driven candidates.

responses.point: Linnarsson places cGAS-STING second, as a conceptual advance in innate immunity of broad importance, and treats the unproven clinical translation as secondary to the clarity of the mechanism.
responses.response: The mechanism is elegant and I do not doubt its originality, but I did not rank B009 in my top eight because I am not persuaded it has yet changed medicine in a discernible way, as STING agonists and inhibitors have not delivered an approved drug. The attribution is also unsettled between Barber and Ishikawa for STING and Chen's group for cGAS and cGAMP, with several parallel groups. I would revisit this in some years, and I would ask whether you think basic-science maturity alone is enough.

responses.point: Sandberg ranks B020 (antisense correction of SMN2 splicing, Krainer and Bennett) fourth, as a mechanism-driven therapy that turned a fatal infantile disease into a treatable one, with a clean two-person configuration.
responses.response: I did not rank B020 on my own opening ballot and should say why. It is a compelling and clean story and the clinical effect is dramatic, but Krainer's splicing mechanism and Bennett's chemistry sit within a wider antisense and RNA-therapeutics history, and a prize here would have to decide whether it recognises SMA or the platform. I do not rule it out, but I do not see it overtaking B025 or B047 this year.

uncertainties: Whether the prize should recognise GLP-1 physiology only, or physiology plus drug development, and therefore whether Knudsen or Mojsov takes the third seat.
Whether Habener's absence from the credited names undermines any B025 configuration.
Whether a two-part prize would be better than a single part; I kept one part because a second part would shrink the GLP-1 trio under the three-person limit.
Whether CAR-T (B047) is more fairly resolved with two or three laureates given Eshhar's absence.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for the shortlisted candidates. My nuclear-receptor and dopamine-neuron work does not overlap with any shortlisted discovery. My profile records past co-authorship with Ronald Evans and collaborations with Johan Ericson, Per Svenningsson and Abdel El Manira, none of whom is a credited name on the shortlist, and these colleague relationships do not require recusal.
